name: Epoch AI (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: an AI catastrophe kills people everywhere and the future lost is everyone's, so the result is spread by world population.
summary: Epoch AI (San Francisco) tracks and forecasts the trajectory of AI: public databases of AI models, compute, chips and data centres, capability benchmarks (FrontierMath, the Epoch Capabilities Index), research reports and a newsletter, used by governments, central banks and journalists, plus paid work for AI companies, investors and governments. This model covers all its work in 2025, its first year as an independent charity ($5M spent, from its impact report; no audited statement for the year is public yet). At the defaults it averts about 0.07 years of healthy life per $1,000, from 0.001 to 0.9 on the model's own ranges, so the result is mostly uncertainty: each dollar of the work that bears on catastrophic risk is valued as a typical project's cut in the forecast risk of an AI catastrophe (Rethink Priorities' cross-cause model, the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament's experts), deaths valued like every death and the future lost counted through the discount rate. It is under a tenth of its cause's median, close to METR's, because Epoch's mission is understanding AI rather than reducing its risks (about 60% of the work counted as bearing on them, at 0.8 of a typical project's uptake), little of it is aimed at misuse (1.7% of spending, under 3% of the counted work: its biological AI tracking, which still gives about two thirds of the result), its benchmarks and paid work for AI companies and investors are taken to speed the race (−9% of the value, −30% of the part they concern), clients' fees for commissioned work are credited to the clients, and the next dollar counts at 23% of the past average after Coefficient Giving's $22.7M in October 2026. The chance of an AI catastrophe (the slider), the typical cut per dollar, the years a cut counts and the share of work counted as misuse are the biggest swings; the one branch is discounted for missing data: no outcome of the work on the risk is measured.

rows.label: AI: share of all spending on work against misuse
rows.explainer: The share of Epoch's 2025 spending aimed at people using AI to do harm. Only one line is: tracking biological AI models (tools that design proteins or advise on lab work), funded by Sentinel Bio ($85,000 in September 2025, $80,000 in 2024, the funding page): $85,000 of $5M, 1.7%, our judgment that the grant pays for the work it names. rows.label: AI: share of the counted (catastrophe-relevant) AI work aimed at misuse
rows.explainer: The misuse work (ai_misuse_spend_share, all of it catastrophe-relevant) over the share of the work counted (catastrophe_relevant_share): about 0.017 / 0.6 = 2.8%. It weights Rethink's misuse preset against its misalignment one inside the counted work. The share matters: for catastrophes the world survives, Rethink's typical misuse project cuts deaths far more per dollar than its misalignment one, so these few percent give about two thirds of the result.

AI work: share of Epoch's work that bears on catastrophic risk
rows.explainer: Not all of Epoch's work is about the risks counted here. Bearing on them: the compute, chip and data-centre trackers, capability benchmarks and the Capabilities Index (how fast dangerous abilities arrive), and the trend research on scaling and timelines that governments and the field plan around. Not bearing on them: the economics work (the GATE growth model's investment advice, enterprise adoption, robotics), the power-demand report commissioned by EPRI, consultations for investors (Sequoia Capital, Bridgewater Associates) and data for the AI Index. About 60%, our judgment from the 2025 outputs the impact report lists (four Data Explorers, the Benchmarking Hub and FrontierMath Tier 4 relevant; most Gradient Updates and Data Insights mixed), 35% to 80%; as GovAI's 80% for a governance organisation, lower because Epoch's mission is understanding AI's trajectory, not reducing its risks. The rest's good is in unmodelled_benefits_adj.

rows.label: AI work: the relevant work's uptake against a typical AI project
rows.explainer: Epoch's catastrophe-relevant work against Rethink Priorities' typical small AI project (a safety project aimed at the risk). Above typical in reach: 987,000 website users and 107 notable mentions in media and reports in 2025, work cited by the Federal Reserve, the IMF, the IEA, the Bank of England, OECD.AI and the US Congressional Research Service, briefings for US congresspeople and the UK AI directorate, consultations with the UK AI Security Institute and the EU AI Office (impact report). Below in aim: it is 'decidedly neutral' on whether advancing AI benefits society and makes no policy recommendations (What is Epoch?), so its effect on the risk runs through others choosing to act on better information, which can go either way (the harms are in speedup_harm_share). 0.8, our judgment, 0.3 to 1.2, below METR's 1.2 (evaluations labs act on before release) and GovAI's 1 (advice aimed at the risk).

Several were paid across 2024 and 2025 (the funding page dates OpenAI's FrontierMath, the Google DeepMind report, the AI Index, EPRI and DSIT '2024/25'), so the fees' share is taken over both years: raised $10.3M in 2025 and about $7.36M in 2024 ('+40% from 2024'), $17.66M, less the gifts the funding page dates to those years ($4.21M in 2024: Coefficient Giving $4,132,488, Sentinel Bio $80,000; $9.955M in 2025: Coefficient Giving $8.5M and $70,000, Jaan Tallinn $600,000, Likith Govindaiah $400,000, Leopold Aschenbrenner $200,000, Girish Sastry $100,000, Sentinel Bio $85,000), about $3.5M of fees, 19.8% of receipts, × the $5M spent = about $990,000. $350,000 (2025's receipts alone) to $1.9M (2024's unlisted receipts all fees and paid for 2025's work): gifts under $70,000 the page leaves out, or grants recognised in another year, move it either way; Epoch says it charges 'at least on par with industry consultants'. Paid work bought by clients is their resources behind the outputs, credited in ai_attribution_share.

rows.label: AI work: Epoch's share against outside contributors

rows.label: Benefits not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Good beyond the catastrophes counted: the work left out by catastrophe_relevant_share (economics of AI, power demand, adoption) informs central banks, energy planners and labour-market policy (the Federal Reserve, the IMF, the IEA and the Bank of England cited it in 2025), and better public understanding of AI helps governments handle its everyday harms. 10% of the modelled value, our judgment, 0 to 30%, as METR's 10%.

rows.label: Harm: speeding up dangerous capabilities, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Beyond a typical project's backfire (in the shared cut): Epoch's work is clearly riskier than typical in three ways. (1) Benchmarks the labs race on: FrontierMath was commissioned by OpenAI (Tier 4 in 2025), which holds most of its problems, and Epoch evaluates models for xAI and Google DeepMind; capability benchmarks give developers targets. (2) Paid work for AI companies and investors: 'AI in 2030' for Google DeepMind, research on RL scaling for Sequoia Capital, consultations for Bridgewater Associates; trend forecasts can pull money into AI and sharpen the race. (3) In April 2025 a co-founder and three staff left to found Mechanize, a start-up that builds training environments and data to enable 'the full automation of the economy', and the work's neutrality on whether faster AI is good means it is not steered away from acceleration. On the value of the work these channels concern, about −30%, the top of the template's anchor for capabilities-adjacent work (−10% to −30%; METR's evaluations −10%), −5% to −60%. But this row is a share of all modelled value, and about two thirds of it comes from the biological AI tracking (ai_misuse_cost_share), which speeds nothing up; so −30% × about 0.3 = −9%, our judgment, −1.5% to −18%.

rows.label: Harm: information hazards and attention, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Beyond a typical project's backfire: Epoch publishes no threat analyses or red-teaming results; its tracker of biological AI models lists public tools and their developers, which could point a bad actor to them, but they are already public. 0, down to −5%, our judgment.
